topic.subject: science
topic.title: Separation of substances
topic.scope: handpicking, winnowing, sieving, sedimentation, decantation, filtration, evaporation, saturated solutions

misconceptions.statement: Handpicking is only used to remove unwanted dirt or stones from food.
misconceptions.why: Students usually see their parents handpicking stones from rice or dal, which are waste items.
misconceptions.fix: Handpicking can be used to separate any two components that are large enough and look different, even if both are useful.

probe.question: If you have a mixture of red beads and green beads, can you use handpicking to separate them?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because neither bead is dirt or waste.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Winnowing only works if there is natural wind blowing outside.
misconceptions.why: Textbook illustrations usually show farmers standing in an open field with wind.
misconceptions.fix: Winnowing requires moving air, which can be provided by a fan or even by moving the mixture through the air manually.

probe.question: Can a farmer separate husk from grain inside a room with a ceiling fan?
probe.wrong_answer: No, winnowing needs natural wind from the sky.

misconceptions.root_belief: natural processes require specific natural conditions

misconceptions.statement: A sieve can separate a mixture of salt and sand because they are both solids.
misconceptions.why: Students think sieving works for any two dry powders without considering particle size.
misconceptions.fix: Sieving only works if the components have different sizes; if salt and sand grains are the same size, they will both pass through.

probe.question: If salt and sand grains are the same size, will a sieve separate them?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the sieve will catch the sand and let the salt pass.

misconceptions.root_belief: processes that look similar are the same

misconceptions.statement: Heavier solids will always sink to the bottom of a liquid immediately.
misconceptions.why: Students observe stones sinking in water and generalize this to all heavy objects.
misconceptions.fix: Sedimentation takes time, and very fine heavy particles may stay suspended for a long time before settling.

probe.question: If you stir fine heavy clay in water, will it settle the moment you stop stirring?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because clay is heavier than water.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Decantation is a perfect way to get completely pure and clear water from a muddy mixture.
misconceptions.why: Students see the top layer looking clearer and assume all impurities are gone.
misconceptions.fix: Decantation only removes the bulk of the liquid; fine suspended particles often remain, requiring filtration.

probe.question: Is the water poured out after sedimentation of mud safe and pure enough to drink?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because all the mud has settled at the bottom.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Filtration can be used to separate dissolved sugar or salt from water.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse 'insoluble' with 'dissolved' and think a fine enough filter catches everything.
misconceptions.fix: Dissolved substances break into particles so small that they pass through the pores of any filter paper.

probe.question: If you pour a clear sugar solution through a filter paper, what will be left on the paper?
probe.wrong_answer: The sugar crystals will be caught by the paper.

misconceptions.root_belief: small things behave like large things

misconceptions.statement: Any piece of paper can be used as a filter in the laboratory.
misconceptions.why: The name 'filter paper' leads students to believe it is just ordinary paper used for filtering.
misconceptions.fix: Filter paper has specific microscopic pores that allow liquids to pass while trapping solids; ordinary paper is too dense or lacks these pores.

probe.question: Can we use a page from your notebook to filter muddy water effectively?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is paper and will act as a filter.

misconceptions.root_belief: objects with same names have same properties

misconceptions.statement: When a salt solution evaporates, the salt also disappears or turns into gas.
misconceptions.why: Students observe the whole liquid 'disappearing' and assume the mixture behaves as a single substance.
misconceptions.fix: Only the liquid turns into vapor; the dissolved solid has a much higher boiling point and remains behind as crystals.

probe.question: If you leave a bowl of salt water in the sun until it dries, what will you find in the bowl?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, because the salt evaporated with the water.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Evaporation only happens when water is boiling at 100 degrees Celsius.
misconceptions.why: Students associate steam and vapor only with boiling kettles or stoves.
misconceptions.fix: Evaporation is a surface process that happens at all temperatures, which is why wet clothes dry even in the shade.

probe.question: Does a puddle of water on the road evaporate only if the sun heats it to boiling point?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, water must boil to turn into vapor.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: A saturated solution is a solid or a very thick paste.
misconceptions.why: The word 'saturated' sounds like 'full' or 'heavy', leading to a confusion of states.
misconceptions.fix: A saturated solution is still a liquid; it is simply a solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that specific temperature.

probe.question: If a salt solution is saturated, what does it look like?
probe.wrong_answer: It looks like a thick solid paste.

misconceptions.root_belief: confusing a state with a process

misconceptions.statement: Stirring a solution faster will eventually allow you to dissolve an infinite amount of salt.
misconceptions.why: Students see stirring helps things 'disappear' and think more effort equals more capacity.
misconceptions.fix: Stirring only helps the solute dissolve faster; it does not change the maximum amount that can dissolve.

probe.question: If you have a saturated solution with salt at the bottom, will stirring it very fast for an hour dissolve that salt?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, fast stirring can dissolve any amount of salt.

misconceptions.root_belief: more effort leads to more results

misconceptions.statement: Heating a solution only makes the salt dissolve faster, but it doesn't change how much can dissolve.
misconceptions.why: Students think of heat as a 'speeder' rather than a factor that changes the property of the solvent.
misconceptions.fix: Heating actually increases the solubility of most solids, meaning a hot liquid can hold more dissolved solid than a cold one.

probe.question: If you heat a saturated salt solution, can you add and dissolve more salt into it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it will just dissolve the existing salt faster.

misconceptions.statement: Condensation on the outside of a cold glass is water that leaked through the glass.
misconceptions.why: Students see water appearing where there was none and assume it came from inside the container.
misconceptions.fix: Water vapor in the air turns into liquid droplets when it touches a cold surface; it does not come from inside the glass.

probe.question: Where do the water droplets on the outside of a cold steel glass come from?
probe.wrong_answer: The water seeped through the tiny pores in the steel.

misconceptions.root_belief: matter can pass through solid barriers

misconceptions.statement: Sedimentation only works for mud and water mixtures.
misconceptions.why: Muddy water is the most common example used in schools and textbooks.
misconceptions.fix: Sedimentation works for any mixture where an insoluble solid is heavier than the liquid, such as sand in water or tea leaves.

probe.question: Can we use sedimentation to separate a mixture of heavy metal filings and oil?
probe.wrong_answer: No, sedimentation is only for cleaning muddy water.

misconceptions.root_belief: a process only applies to one example

misconceptions.statement: A sieve with larger holes is always better because it works faster.
misconceptions.why: Students prioritize speed and efficiency over the accuracy of separation.
misconceptions.fix: The hole size must be smaller than the component you want to retain; if holes are too large, the whole mixture will pass through.

probe.question: To separate stones from fine flour, should you use a sieve with very big holes?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the flour will fall through much faster.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
